Unreliable Narrator. A narrative voice whose account of events cannot be trusted because of deliberate deception, mental illness, limited perspective, or moral blindness. The reader must become a detective, constructing truth from distortion.

Edgar Allan Poe's The Tell-Tale Heart is the canonical example. The narrator insists he is not mad while describing his methodical murder of an old man. He becomes obsessed with the sound of the dead man's heart still beating somewhere in the house, haunting him. The narrator's very defense—his insistence on his sanity—proves the opposite. We see the contradiction he cannot see in himself. He is mad precisely because he cannot recognize his own madness.

Agatha Christie's The Murder of Roger Ackroyd does something different. The narrator tells the truth about events but withholds a crucial fact. The reader is technically not lied to directly, but deliberately misled through omission. The detective work is reading between the lines, understanding what silence conceals.

Unreliability can stem from different sources. Madness distorts perception. The narrator genuinely misunderstands reality. Deception means the narrator lies deliberately. Limited knowledge means the narrator simply lacks access to full information. Bias means the narrator's values distort their judgment. Each creates different kinds of unreliability.

The effect is dramatic irony. The reader knows or suspects the narrator is wrong. The pleasure comes from solving the puzzle beneath the false account. We read alongside the narrator and independently of the narrator, verifying or contradicting what they tell us. This creates tension and engagement that a reliable narrator cannot.

It's important to distinguish unreliability from other kinds of narrative limitation. An ignorant narrator simply doesn't know what's happening. An innocent narrator misunderstands correctly. An unreliable narrator actively misleads. The last creates a specific kind of dramatic pleasure, a puzzle the reader must solve.

In modernist and postmodern literature, unreliability becomes a formal technique reflecting doubt about knowledge itself. The idea that truth is unstable and contested, that what we know is always mediated through perspective and limitation. First-person narrative is particularly susceptible to unreliability. It naturally restricts perspective. The narrator's reliability becomes a central question. Can you trust what you're being told? What are they hiding? What can't they see about themselves? These questions drive the narrative forward.
